clue.text: Rock cake? That's nutty sweet !

explanation.surface: A question about a rock cake, answered as if it were a confection with nuts in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Rock cake' literally: something rock-hard that has been baked. The same compound is also the name of an almond toffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock-hard baking describes the first sense; the second is an old name for a brittle almond toffee.

clue.text: A harvester who is chirpy when he rests on the grass

definitions.text: A harvester who is chirpy when he rests on the grass

parts.words: A harvester who is chirpy when he rests on the grass
parts.note: a picker of hops is a harvester; put grass before the word and you get the chirping insect

explanation.surface: A cheerful farm worker lying on the grass in his break.
explanation.walkthrough: A hop-picker harvests hops; set 'grass' before the word, as it rests on it, and the chirping insect appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker who picks hops in the harvest, and the second half of the chirping insect's name.

clue.text: "Where the apples Never pry "(Browning)

parts.note: a gap-fill from Browning's poem A Woman's Last Word, in which the missing verb tells what ripe apples do

explanation.surface: A line of Robert Browning with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a blank: 'Where the apple ——s, Never pry'. Browning's line is 'Where the apple reddens, Never pry', from A Woman's Last Word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripening apples turn crimson, the verb the poet used for them.

clue.text: Dinna ye hear it? " (What a relief !)

definitions.text: Dinna ye hear it? " (What a relief !)

parts.words: Dinna ye hear it? " (What a relief !)
parts.note: the cry of Jessie Brown at the Relief of Lucknow in 1857, hearing the Highland regiments' pipes approaching

explanation.surface: A Scots voice asking if you hear something, and the sigh of relief that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: The story of the Relief of Lucknow in 1857 has a Scottish woman cry 'Dinna ye hear it?' as the pipes of the relieving Highlanders sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish reed instrument with a windbag whose sound announced the relieving troops.

clue.text: One may be bound to

parts.note: a magistrate can bind someone over, that is, legally oblige them to behave well

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' is the legal sense: a court can bind a person over to behave lawfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Being bound over by a court means pledging to behave and avoid any disturbance of public order.

clue.text: Play possible here, though a tree is in the way

indicators.note: the tree is said to be in the way, so its letters sit inside the letters for way

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the pine is a tree

explanation.surface: A spot fit for play, if only a tree were not blocking it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small keyboard instrument, the harpsichord's cousin, is something on which music is played.

clue.text: Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme

parts.note: Moliere's comedy about Monsieur Jourdain, a newly rich tradesman aping the nobility

explanation.walkthrough: Moliere's play mocks a newly rich merchant trying to pass as a gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-made upstart with new money who wants social rank, like Moliere's would-be gentleman.

clue.text: Trousers to one girl are lamentable it seems

parts.note: Nan is a girl's name
to keen is to wail or lament, read here as the girl's sorrowful sounds

explanation.surface: A remark that trousers would make a certain girl weep.
explanation.walkthrough: To keen is to wail in mourning, an Irish custom at funerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers made of a yellowish cotton cloth from Nanjing.

clue.text: Valley of small sandhills?

parts.note: golf tees were once little mounds of sand, and dale means valley

explanation.surface: A question about a valley full of dunes.
explanation.walkthrough: Golfers once teed off from small heaps of sand, so 'small sandhills' are tees; a dale is a valley. The result is the valley of the river Tees in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The dale of the river Tees in northern England, read as a valley of golf tees.

clue.text: A source of Pooh-Bah's pride- Gee, it was pre-Adamite !

definitions.text: A source of Pooh-Bah's pride- Gee, it was pre-Adamite !

parts.words: A source of Pooh-Bah's pride- Gee, it was pre-Adamite !
parts.note: Pooh-Bah, the haughty official in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, boasts of his family descent from before Adam

explanation.surface: An exclamation of wonder at how far back Pooh-Bah's proud family line goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Pooh-Bah calls himself 'of pre-Adamite ancestral descent', so what he is proud of is his line of ancestors.
explanation.definitionFit: A recorded line of ancestry is what a family's pride in its descent rests on.

clue.text: Stupor of one under the influence of spirits

definitions.text: Stupor of one under the influence of spirits

parts.words: Stupor of one under the influence of spirits
parts.note: reads like a drunk's daze, but the spirits are ghosts and the person is a medium at a seance

explanation.surface: A drinker's daze after too much whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' suggests alcohol; the state meant is a medium's, possessed by the spirits of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A medium at a seance falls into a dazed, hypnotic state while the dead supposedly speak.

clue.text: Imitate the action of the pendulum seemingly ill

definitions.text: Imitate the action of the pendulum seemingly ill

parts.words: Imitate the action of the pendulum seemingly ill
parts.note: a pendulum is a swinging weight of metal, and the idiom means to shirk work by pretending to be ill

explanation.surface: A clock's pendulum mimicked by someone who looks unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom, British slang for malingering, describes literally what a weighted pendulum does.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for shirking by faking sickness, read literally as moving a weight back and forth.

clue.text: Gray type

parts.note: Thomas Gray wrote the famous Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, so a Gray type is a writer of mournful poems

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' looks like a colour; it is the poet Thomas Gray, best known for his Elegy.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet writing laments for the dead, as Gray did in his churchyard poem.

clue.text: Jam today and tomorrow in the holiday season !

definitions.text: Jam today and tomorrow in the holiday season !

parts.words: Jam today and tomorrow in the holiday season !
parts.note: the jam is a traffic jam, filling the roads on Saturday and Sunday when everyone drives out

explanation.surface: A treat of jam promised for today and tomorrow during the holidays, as in Alice's 'jam tomorrow'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam today' recalls Lewis Carroll's 'jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today'; here it is road traffic over two days off.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturday and Sunday, the two days of leisure when roads clog with traffic.

clue.text: It's not a result of the Bore

definitions.text: It's not a result of the Bore

parts.words: It's not a result of the Bore
parts.note: the Severn Bore is a tidal wave on that river; the railway passage under the river was bored by engineers, not by the wave

explanation.surface: Denying that something was caused by a tedious person.
explanation.walkthrough: The Severn Bore is a tidal surge up the River Severn in western England; the railway passage beneath that river was bored by people, so it is not the work of the Bore.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway passage beneath the river estuary, made by boring through rock rather than by the tidal wave.

clue.text: Everlasting flower

parts.note: poets named an imaginary unfading bloom, and a real plant with long-lasting red tassels shares the name

explanation.definitionFit: An imaginary bloom that never fades, in poetry, and a real plant with lasting red tassels.

clue.text: Sounds to have been a lively wedding of Miss Laurie's

indicators.note: the clue says the phrase sounds like the word, so it is to be said out loud

parts.note: Annie Laurie is the heroine of a famous Scottish song, so her wedding would be Annie mated

explanation.surface: Gossip that Miss Laurie's wedding was a lively affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annie Laurie' is a well-known Scottish love song; 'Annie mated', said out loud, gives the word for lively.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of life and energy, as in spirited conversation.

clue.text: Post Office pundit ?

parts.note: a postman handles letters all day, but the pundit meant is a scholar and writer

explanation.surface: A know-all at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: Letters here are literature, not mail: the expert is a learned author.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary scholar or author, an expert in writing rather than in the post.

clue.text: Connoisseur of the Decorated Style ?

parts.note: Decorated is a phase of English Gothic architecture; the word for a keen judge or breeder also means more ornate

explanation.surface: An expert on the Decorated phase of Gothic church building.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means an expert breeder or enthusiast, and also 'more ornate', which suits a decorated style.
explanation.definitionFit: A keen judge or breeder of something, and the comparative of ornate.

clue.text: What a game for drivers with stiff necks !

definitions.text: What a game for drivers with stiff necks !

parts.words: What a game for drivers with stiff necks !
parts.note: backing a car up means twisting round to look behind, painful with a stiff neck

explanation.surface: Grumbling about how hard backing up is for motorists with sore necks.
explanation.walkthrough: The board game, played with counters that flip colour, takes its name from turning over; drivers who back up must turn their heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A board game of flipping counters, its name suggesting backing a car up.

clue.text: Elizabeth I gets round to transposing an air

parts.note: a round shape is a ring, the letter O

indicators.note: the words an air are transposed, their letters moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth I getting round to arranging a tune in another key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transposing' rearranges AN AIR into RIANA. 'Transposing an air' sounds musical, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriana was the poetic name for the Virgin Queen in Elizabethan madrigals.

clue.text: Panda as pineapple

annotationWithheld.why: Panda as pineapple (6): the scan agrees with the held text; 'pineapple' defines ANANAS, but no reading of 'Panda as' builds the letters (not hidden, not an anagram, no homophone found)

clue.text: Latin or in turn, madly excited

indicators.note: the word or is turned round, so its letters are read backwards

parts.note: manic means wildly or madly excited

explanation.surface: Someone choosing between Latin and a state of frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in turn' turns OR into RO.
explanation.definitionFit: Romance languages descend from the speech of ancient Rome, so they are of Latin origin.

clue.text: Come around, neighbour!

explanation.surface: A call to a neighbour to drop by.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs here: to encircle, and to lie near or border on.
explanation.definitionFit: To encircle or surround something is to come around it; to border on or lie beside a place is to neighbour it.

clue.text: Hair grease ?

parts.note: nut is slang for the head, so a lubricant for the head would be a head oil, and a real kind of oil pressed from kernels

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is slang for the head; oil pressed from kernels is also a real product.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil pressed from walnuts or other kernels, read as oil for the head.

clue.text: Worcester doctor-repellent

parts.note: Worcester is a variety of apple, and an apple a day keeps the doctor away

explanation.walkthrough: 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away'; the Worcester is a variety of red English dessert apple.
explanation.definitionFit: A variety of eating apple, the fruit that proverbially keeps the doctor away.

clue.text: He would take an age to climb the wall

parts.note: he would contracts to he'd
an era is an age

explanation.surface: A man who would spend ages getting over a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a plant that does the climbing: the botanical name for ivy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is the plant that climbs walls, and this is its Latin genus name.

clue.text: Madam Butterfly might have been even more attracted to one of these

definitions.text: Madam Butterfly might have been even more attracted to one of these

parts.words: Madam Butterfly might have been even more attracted to one of these
parts.note: the opera heroine fell for Pinkerton, a naval lieutenant; a butterfly might also be drawn to the red butterfly species named after senior naval officers

explanation.surface: Puccini's heroine, who loved a mere navy lieutenant, would have loved a higher rank even more.
explanation.walkthrough: In Puccini's opera, Cio-Cio-San loves Lieutenant Pinkerton of the US Navy; a real butterfly is drawn to its own kind, and the Red Admiral is a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-ranking naval officers, outranking a lieutenant, and also a family of butterflies such as the red one.
